firms and community forums. The community echoed the market’s features, spread the

word and engage in actions that got noticed by external audiences, media, potential users,

which made firms very attractive.



                                      39Firms’ reputation is important to convince users, potential employees, suppliers, etc., but

the social interactions among members in the community extended the social influence and

more people started to pay attention to the new market. The corresponding proposition as

follows:

       P2. Firms-community interactions that use reputation-enhanced mechanisms (i.e.

       storytelling-community’s   replication,  emotional  appeal-responsiveness  and

       leadership signals-community’s  skills, enthusiasm) are more likely to achieve

       higher levels of awareness and perception of worth for the product/market in the

      mind of market audiences as compared to firm only strategies.



2.5.3. Knowledge sourcing interactions

Knowledge sourcing interactions are important sources of knowledge about users’ current

and future needs. Knowledge sourcing outside the firm fosters innovative outcomes

(Chesbrough, 2006) and firms can get the resources and technical skills relevant in the

development of technological products of a new market/category (Haefliger, Jäger and von

Krogh, 2010). However, unless the knowledge is strategic, sourcing is not necessarily

advantageous; it could be time-consuming and demands attention (Einsenhardt and Santos,

2002; Laursen and  Salter, 2006), even more many product innovators  fail to link

technological issues to market related issues (Dougherty, 1992).

Knowledge sourcing interactions generate user knowledge about current products and

future needs, i.e. the new market potential. In nascent markets, knowledge changes fast, is

sticky and difficult to validate, the use of the products provides users with informational

advantages (e.g. valuable features, how the products work with other products, etc.), so

users articulate the needs about products and help to generate interest that ultimately allows

the creation of the new market (Shah and Tripsas, 2012; West and O’Mahony, 2005).

Accessibility to product’s information and the creation of their own projects with the

product allow community members to detect problems, recombine ideas and develop new

functions. Additionally, community members help other users in forums and voice future

product wants and although firms take the final decisions, both firms and user community

converge towards a common perception of what is valuable (Dahlander, 2007; Dahlander,

Frederiksen, & Rullani, 2008).




                                      40The users’ feedback allows entrepreneurs to select new goals that enrich their identity and

helps to distinguish the firm and the market, e.g. Arduino got from its users the interest for

new developments towards robots and Internet of things. SeeedStudio identified problems

of Arduino’s product from users and launched  its own improved product. SparkFun

periodically reviews users’ demands to create and launch products and extended its existing

business to building kits and to education. The product and user knowledge generated are

a key source for renewal, something that strengthen the ability to create value (Rindova and

Fombrun, 1999).

       P3. Firms-community interactions that support knowledge exchange are more likely

        to provide knowledge about users’ current and future needs and consequently

       strengthen the ability to create value.



2.5.4. Market acceptance

The previously described  sets of  interactions explain  actions of entrepreneurs and

community members that have an impact on the market emergence. This reinforces research

stating that sustained social interactions with communities can become intangible assets

and a source of competitive advantage (Fosfuri et al., 2010; Rindova and Fombrun, 1999).

But before that happens, firms have to learn how to manage the relationship with the

community and to develop the ability to convene community members to participate, to

gather feedback and to select improvements without alienating the community.

In the creation of markets, there are elements of judgments, evaluation and social

construction of reality. However, in high uncertainty and ambiguity environments, the bases

for comparing products are as unclear as the relevant knowledge about the firms to be

evaluated (Navis and Glynn, 2010; Khaire, 2014). Entrepreneurs provide a cognitive

framing but the constant interactions of relevant actors generate a shared understanding of

the product/market and its value (Khaire, 2014). This happened with OSHW firms and their

communities. The firms grew with the community and vice versa. The user communities

became relevant actors, actively participating in the creation of value.

The ongoing interactions improved the chances of success (West and O’Mahony, 2005), by

providing the means to understand the functions and the utility of the products. And when

actors do not question the usefulness of a new product or the value of the industry it

represents, the new industry is accepted or taken for granted (Rao, 1994; Zucker, 1983).

                                      41The evidence of a shared acceptance of OSHW goes from products included in the schools

curricula to the increasing offer of clones and derivatives. Derivatives can create confusion

in users, but a strong identity helped to distinguish between boards of similar or identical

design from different producers (Mellis, 2014). The corresponding proposition as follows:

       Proposition  4. New  entrants  that over time  proactively engage  in  identity,

       reputation and knowledge sourcing related interactions with communities are more

        likely to achieve the acceptance of the market by market-audiences.



2.6. Discussion

Prior research on market creation has found strategies based on dominance using cognitive

and competitive mechanisms (Santos and Eisenhardt, 2009) and use of mechanisms such

as identity that facilitate the social construction of it (Khaire, 2014; Navis and Glynn, 2011).

In a way those studies consider both internal (entrepreneurial) and external (audience)

factors. However, this study differs from this body of research in the peculiarities of firms

producing physical open source products and in the inclusion of user communities, actively

involved in the construction of the market. They play a different role than other types of

communities such as financial security analysts and market investors (Navis and Glynn,

2010). I propose a framework based o

                        Rahul Guhathakurta1and Ruben Nag2



Introduction

In June 2025, Prusa Research a.s. signed a related-party report stating that the companies in its
group develop and manufacture all components themselves (Prusa Research  a.s., 2025).
Eighteen months earlier, its founder, Josef Průša, had written: "You will find parts sourced from
China in our printers because some components are manufactured in sufficient quantities only
there" (Průša, 2024). The two statements are not necessarily inconsistent. The first is a legal
description of who designs and makes the components that the group sells. The second is an
engineer's admission that a printer is assembled from parts some of which no European firm
makes at the required volume. The gap between them is a useful place to begin a case about
how open the Prague-based maker of the Original Prusa 3D printers really is, and about what
that openness does and does not protect.

strategy and resilience, risk modeling, and the intersection of technology, manufacturing, and enterprise decision-
making.

2 Ruben Nag is a Strategy Consultant at IBM, Kolkata, specialising in global finance and supply chain strategy.
With over nine years of experience, he focuses on solving complex problems, making things happen and creating
real value across industries.

Prusa Research grew out of the RepRap movement, in which printer designs were shared
openly so that anyone could build, copy and improve them. By 2024 the group was processing
about 300,000 orders a year and its team exceeded 1,000 people (Prusa Research, 2025a). Five
of its operating companies reported combined revenue of about CZK 6.6 billion in 2024 before
intra-group eliminations (Prusa Research a.s., 2025; Prusa Manufacturing a.s., 2025). Over the
same period, the desktop printer market changed around it. Lower-priced enclosed CoreXY
printers, many made by firms headquartered in China, reached the market at a fraction of
Prusa's price, and by the first quarter of 2026 four companies (Bambu Lab, Creality, Elegoo
and Anycubic) shipped 88 per cent of entry-level units worldwide (CONTEXT, 2026). In
August 2025 Průša published an essay entitled "Open hardware desktop 3D printing is dead –
you just don't know it yet" (Průša, 2025). Four months later the company released the full CAD
model of its CORE One printer under a new licence of its own design, the Open Community
License (OCL), which permits use and modification but restricts commercial resale (Prusa
Research, 2025c).

The case asks how an open-source hardware company can turn community-driven innovation
into durable commercial advantage while scaling manufacturing, protecting quality and
sustaining supply continuity in a market where lower-priced competitors can learn from what
it publishes. It does so through the lens of what this case calls the qualification bottleneck: the
firm's scarce capacity to test, validate and certify parts, suppliers and code. The proposition is
that this capability may be both the main barrier to imitation and the main limit on resilience,
because publishing a design makes copying cheaper for rivals but does not make switching
suppliers cheaper for the firm itself. The case does not resolve that tension. It presents the
evidence available on 15 August 2026, a quantitative teaching model and seven strategic
options, and leaves the choice to the reader.

From RepRap to a Group of Specialised Companies
Josef Průša began building printers within the RepRap project before founding Prusa Research
in Prague in 2012, according to the company's 2024 annual report (Prusa Research a.s., 2025).
The firm's early products, the Original Prusa i3 family, were sold as kits and assembled printers,
with printed parts, firmware and electronics published under open licences. The open-frame
MK3S+ and the compact MINI were released with full manufacturing data for their circuit
boards (Prusa Research, 2026c). Exhibit 1 summarises the developments relevant to this case.

What Prusa Opens, and What It Keeps
Prusa's openness is layered rather than total. The slicer, PrusaSlicer, is published under the
GNU Affero General Public License (AGPL-3.0), and its code has been reused by other firms;
Bambu Studio and the community slicer OrcaSlicer descend from  it (The Verge, 2025).
Firmware for the current 32-bit Buddy boards is published under the GNU General Public
License, while some graphics carry a non-commercial Creative Commons licence. Printed parts
are published as STEP and STL files. For the MK4, MK4S, CORE One and CORE One L, the
company's open-source page lists schematics as released but manufacturing data and most bills
of materials as withheld (Prusa Research, 2026c). In March 2023 Průša explained that the
MK4's electronics would be held back until a licence existed that would limit what he described
as direct cloning (Průša, 2023). Critics in the open-hardware community argued that this
weakened the case for calling the product open at all (Weinberg, 2023). The December 2025
OCL release of the CORE One CAD model was presented by Prusa as open-sourcing; critics

The Competitive Field at the Cut-off
The desktop segment in which Prusa sells is no longer the hobbyist niche of the early RepRap
years. CONTEXT, an industry analysis firm, reported that entry-level printer shipments
(systems under US$2,500) grew by 39 per cent year on year in the first quarter of 2026 and
accounted for 54 per cent of all printer system revenue; the four largest vendors held 88 per
cent of entry-level units, and Flashforge grew fastest, by more than 120 per cent (CONTEXT,
2026). CONTEXT does not report Prusa's share, and Průša's January 2024 reference to roughly
10 per cent of the home segment rested on unnamed estimates (Průša, 2024); no comparable
share figure is used in this case. Creality's Hong Kong prospectus, published on 20 May 2026,
provides audited figures for one rival (Creality, 2026b); Bambu Lab is privately held and
figures attributed to it in the press are unaudited.

The vast number of different ways that OSHW development can be
performed makes it impossible to draw very broad positive or neg-
ative conclusions. Additionally, only so much can be backed up by
the survey and the interviews without delving into completely un-
substantiated discussion. What can be substantiated from the survey
results follows;
   • Improvements to an OSHW device from non-commercial users
      are likely often fed back into the original device, where changes
      are often made as a hobby, as part of an education, or for plea-
      sure.

   •  It is likely that many of the non-commercial users are students
    and use OSHW as a part of their education.

   • Commercial users of OSHW are very pragmatic and the total cost
      of adoption is important. OSHW devices are usually regarded as
     having poor documentation and support.

   • There is the potential for OSHW documentation to be regarded
     as very good; many users stated that the ability to study the
     inner workings of a device is very important both in the numer-
       ical part of the survey and in the comment section.

   • Existing commercial developers of OSHW primarily use existing
     devices as a base for developing a new device rather than incre-
     mental or minor changes.

   • In general, all survey groups rated OSHW devices highly, mak-
     ing it likely that among audiences similar to that of the survey
     the added value of a device being OSHW is high.

   •  It is possible that OSHW devices can be very useful in a tech-
      nical research setting; seven of the survey participants (approx-
     imately 1.5%) reported an educational background of holding
     a PhD or higher.  The inherent ﬂexibility of OSHW may ﬁnd
    many applications in research, partly due to the high level of
     customization that is required in novel research and partly due
      to the level of collaboration that is common between different
     teams.

5.3.2.2  Potential Pitfalls when Implementing OSHW Development

Previous research into OSHW (as described in Chapter 2), comments
from the survey, and interview responses are generally in line and
support two primary difﬁculties in commercially developing OSHW.76    discussion


       The foremost issue, brought up by Pololu, the survey comments,
     and Acosta [14], concerns the licensing options available for OSHW15.
     These licenses are often very limited, nearly placing the device in the
      public domain and allowing free use of the non-copyrightable parts
      of a device. This is primarily due to the lack of legal protection for
     hardware that serves the equivalent of copyright for software (which
      allows for the construction of recursive licenses such as the GNU
    GPL [9]). The closest existing license, the TAPR-OHL [3], primarily
      gives protection for patented parts of devices; thereby requiring far
     more effort and ﬁnancial resources for protection. Though patents
      are typically within the ﬁnancial reach of a company, this is primar-
       ily applicable for companies developing few complex devices, rather
      than SparkFun Electronics which develops very many devices.
       The risk of clones in OSHW is brought up in the comment section of
      the survey; where a device is copied by a third party and then sold at
     a very low cost, competing with the original developer whom must re-
      cuperate development costs in order to remain proﬁtable. This behav-
       ior is typically not seen in the OSS world, as OSS is often distributed
       at zero cost, thereby removing any cloning incentive (income being
     most often generated through other channels, such as support or con-
       sulting). Branding, trademarks, manufacturing quality, continuously
     updating devices, and developing new devices are methods that are
      often used by the developer to maintain sales, according to SparkFun
      Electronics (see Section A.1) and Thompson [30].
         Finally, compliance testing of OSHW devices is an aspect that may
     be difﬁcult to solve for business models where community improve-
     ments are integrated into the main device.  SparkFun Electronics
      writes that for most of the devices they sell expensive testing is not
      required, such as kits or sub-assemblies which do not require any
       testing. The Arduino group [5] has developed relatively few main de-
      vices that are certiﬁed and do not change rapidly, while the commu-
      nity instead focuses on developing separate hardware that attaches to
      the main Arduino device, expanding functionality without requiring
      the main device to redo compliance testing. (Of course, the add-in
     boards themselves must undergo some certiﬁcation process before
      they can be sold, though this does not directly inﬂuence the original
      developers).

   Abstract. This is a teaching case inspired by the Czech 3D printer manufacturer Prusa Research,
   particularly its innovative business model based on self-replication. Born out of RepRap, an
   open-source project to design self-replicating 3D printers, Prusa Research successfully marketed
  3D printers whose plastic parts are 3D-printed. What advantages does 3D printing offer over
   injection molding? In this case, students first perform cost-modeling exercises to estimate costs
   of injection molding and 3D printing. They are then guided through a discussion about the
   advantages of 3D printing. This case may be used as a cost-modeling exercise as well as an
   advanced  Operations  Management/Manufacturing  case  to  showcase  the  relevance  of
   conventional Operational concepts in the context of new manufacturing technologies.

  Keywords: 3D printing, additive manufacturing, manufacturing, technology, innovation,
   entrepreneurship, startup, business model, digitalization, digital operations, open source, open
   hardware.


   1.  Prologue

  “This is going to be a long flight,” thought Logan as the airplane took off from
  Dallas, Texas for Prague, Czech Republic. An MBA student at the Naveen
  Jindal School of Management, University of Texas at Dallas and a consultant
   intern, Logan would report his preliminary analysis and recommendations to
  Josef Prusa, co-founder and CEO of Prusa Research1. The project was about
  Prusa Research’s flagship product, the Prusa i3 3D printer (Exhibit 1). Logan’s
  task  was  to  explore  injection  molding  as  a  potential  replacement
  manufacturing technology for the plastic parts of the printer. “Injection
  molding as a replacement manufacturing technology?” Logan remembered the
  confusion as he  first read the assignment. “I’m hard-pressed to think of
  anything plastic that isn’t injection-molded.” He read on with curiosity as for
  what the current manufacturing technology was. When Logan finally found
  out the answer, he gasped in shock and disbelief. The company had been
  producing plastic parts for the Prusa i3 3D printers—by 3D-printing them on

2. 3D Printing

Three-dimensional (3D) printing is a process in which a material is joined or
solidified  layer-upon-layer  under  computer  control  to  create  a  three-
dimensional object. 3D printing is also known as additive manufacturing toOperations Management Education Review 15                                      7

highlight the process of adding layers of the material to form an object, in
contrast with subtractive manufacturing processes such as machining where
the material is removed from a chunk to form an object. The 3D blueprints for
3D printing are either obtained from scanning physical objects or crafted using
computer-aided design (CAD) software. Various technologies have been
developed to 3D-print a range of materials including plastics, metals, food or
even living cells (to form tissues or organs).
   3D printing displays tremendous promises. Its flexibility enables low-cost
and rapid prototyping and personalization: artists, designers and engineers can
easily materialize their digital blueprints during iterative experiments and
improvements, and doctors and apparel makers can make implants, prosthetics
and clothes that perfectly  fit each patient or customer. In addition, the
technology  is  also  used  in  scenarios where  traditional  manufacturing
technologies are ineffective. For example, General Electric (GE)’s aviation
department 3D-prints turbine blades in titanium aluminide (TiAl) for the
GE9X jet engine powering Boeing’s next-generation 777X jets2 (Exhibit 2).
TiAl is a strong, heat-resistant and light material ideal for turbine blades, but it
cannot be machined due to its brittle quality, and molding the material is also
difficult and  expensive. 3D  printing  proves  to be  the most  effective
manufacturing technology for TiAl. Finally, 3D printing is quickly gaining
ground in the construction industry as a cost-effective, versatile, fast and less
wasteful   construction  method3.  However,  where   alternative  mass-
manufacturing technologies such as injection molding and casting are viable,
3D printing has typically not taken over.

3. SLA, SLS, and FDM

Plastics are the earliest and by far the most popular material for 3D printing. In
1981, Hideo Kodama of Nagoya Municipal Industrial Research Institute
invented two additive methods  for  fabricating three-dimensional  plastic
models with photo-hardening thermoset polymer, whereby the liquid resin is
solidified by ultraviolet (UV) exposure, and the exposure area is controlled by
either a mask patter or a scanning fiber transmitter4. Based on this principle,
Charles Hull built the world’s first 3D printer in 1984 and filed the patent for
stereolithography (SLA)5. Because the technology involves liquid resin, the
printing and post-processing (rinsing, curing and drying) can be messy. The
need for a full tank of resin tends to limit the maximum printable size. Objects

## pqac-00000049

From text 'pearce2017emergingbusinessmodels pages 8-9'.

Joshua M. Pearce. Emerging business models for open source hardware. ArXiv, Mar 2017. URL: https://doi.org/10.5334/joh.4, doi:10.5334/joh.4. This article has 160 citations.

The excerpt states that MakerBot was purchased by Stratasys in 2013 for $403 million. After MakerBot moved away from the Open Hardware ethos, it reportedly lost community support and faced customer outrage over licensing changes on Thingiverse, attempts to patent freely uploaded designs, deletion of documentation, and the release of proprietary printers and software. Its proprietary “Smart Extruder” was described as a major engineering failure that led to a class-action lawsuit, while subsequent operational failures contributed to sharply declining sales, layoffs, outsourcing of U.S. manufacturing, and closure of retail locations. In contrast, Aleph Objects, the company behind LulzBot, continued using an open-source model and showed strong performance: it achieved 2,782% three-year revenue growth, ranked #122 in the 2016 Inc. 500, reported $5.8 million in second-quarter 2016 revenue, had four consecutive profitable quarters, and grew to 146 employees. The excerpt contrasts this with MakerBot’s sale of only 1,421 printers during the cited period and concludes that Aleph Objects’ performance suggests remaining open source can be profitable. Prusa Research revenue and growth rates are not mentioned in the provided excerpt.


---

## pqac-00000050

From text 'viseur20223dprinterbuilders’ pages 3-4'.

Robert Viseur and Nicolas Jullien. 3d printer builders’ open-hardware strategies. Proceedings of the 18th International Symposium on Open Collaboration, pages 1-8, Sep 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.1145/3555051.3555069, doi:10.1145/3555051.3555069. This article has 2 citations.

The excerpt describes MakerBot’s transition from RepRap-derived open hardware to a proprietary strategy. MakerBot was incorporated in 2009 to commercialize open designs, but by September 2012 its Replicator 2 was released under a proprietary license. The company also pursued patents beginning in 2010, changed its model-sharing platform’s terms to transfer ownership of creators’ designs to MakerBot, and increasingly relied on proprietary technological assets and a professional-market strategy. The shift provoked opposition from the RepRap community, including calls for a boycott, a halt to contributions, and reverse engineering of proprietary machines. The text attributes the strategic reversal mainly to value-capture difficulties, including losses of low-cost desktop-printer market share to Chinese manufacturers and slower-than-expected market growth. It characterizes MakerBot’s later approach as essentially proprietary, aside from older open-source software and firmware, and compares it with a razor-and-blade model centered on patented modular extruders and associated materials. The excerpt also states that Ultimaker scaled successfully while progressively closing its hardware development process. It does not provide MakerBot’s acquisition price, information about LulzBot/Aleph Objects’ performance, or Prusa Research’s revenue and growth rates; those figures would need to be located elsewhere in the article or in other sources.

It does not give MakerBot’s acquisition price or describe the company’s later financial or market performance. LulzBot/Aleph Objects is not discussed in the supplied pages, so its performance under an open-source model cannot be established from this excerpt. For Prusa Research, the text reports 2024 sales of goods of CZK 3,435.8 million, alongside CZK 216.9 million in sales of its own products and services. Ninety-three percent of goods sales were made abroad, and Prusa Polymers produced more than half a million filament spools. The excerpt characterizes Prusa as primarily a hardware-and-materials business supported by software, rather than a software business with hardware attached. It does not provide Prusa Research’s year-over-year revenue growth rate. A separate figure is reported for Prusa Manufacturing: revenue increased from CZK 1,686.5 million to CZK 2,115.5 million in 2024, while operating result rose from CZK 9.5 million to CZK 66.3 million; however, this is a group manufacturing entity, not necessarily total Prusa Research revenue.

The company also developed installation, customization, and maintenance services for printer farms and diversified revenue through printer sales, an online shop, and recurring filament purchases. {"answer": "## Economics and Commercialization of Open-Source Hardware: A Literature Review

### 1. Cost Savings of Open-Source Scientific Hardware

A substantial body of work, led primarily by Joshua Pearce, has quantified the economic advantages of free and open-source hardware (FOSH) for scientific and laboratory applications. A comprehensive review of 119 open-source hardware articles from the HardwareX and PLOS Open Source Toolkit repositories found that FOSH provides **average savings of 87%** compared with functionally equivalent proprietary equipment (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003). Savings varied by enabling technology: devices built with Arduino-based electronics averaged **89% savings**, those using RepRap-class 3-D printing averaged **92%**, and devices combining both technologies averaged **94%** (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003). These figures compare direct material costs against commercial purchase prices and may understate total value because proprietary cost equivalents were available for only 37.8% of the reviewed devices—some open-source tools had no commercial counterpart (pqac-00000002).

Individual case studies show even more dramatic savings. An open-source spectrophotometer alternative costing $6 replaced a $1,113 commercial system (~99.5% savings), a multi-fluorescence imaging system costing $250 replaced $10,000 equipment (97.5%), and an open-source selective laser sintering system at $10,000 replaced a $400,000 proprietary system (97.5%) (pqac-00000004). An educational optics setup costing approximately $500 replaced $15,000 of commercial equipment, a 96.7% reduction that, if scaled nationally, could save more than $66 million across U.S. physics laboratories, more than $500 million across U.S. secondary schools, and over $1 billion globally (pqac-00000001).

The following table summarizes documented cost comparisons:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

### 2. Return on Investment for Open-Source Scientific Hardware Development

Pearce (2016) demonstrated that publicly funded open-source hardware development can yield extraordinary returns on investment. Using an open-source syringe pump library as a case study, the development cost was estimated at approximately $30,000. Based on download statistics and estimated savings of $153–$1,402 for a single pump and $1,636–$2,442 for a double pump, the total value of the design library exceeded $168,000 within one month and reached more than $2.5 million within one year. This corresponded to calculated ROI values of **460% to more than 8,300%**. When the 52% national-average overhead typically charged to conventional equipment was included, the ROI increased to **750% to more than 12,000%** (pqac-00000000). The study characterized these as conservative estimates because they excluded benefits from improved equipment, education, and scientific productivity.

Pearce (2026) further analyzed four financial models for open hardware development: (1) a philanthropy model where funders bear all design risks; (2) a standard investor model; (3) a crowd-sourced model; and (4) a novel "decoupled risk investor model" that separates design risk from ROI risk by introducing a guarantor. In a hypothetical case study, 100 proprietary bottle rollers costing $2,439 each ($243,925 total) could be replaced with open-source units at approximately $150 each after a $100,000 development investment, saving over $100,000 (pqac-00000035). The article argues that FOSH reduces costs generally by **more than 90%** for equivalent or lesser proprietary hardware while accelerating development through collaborative design (pqac-00000035).

### 3. Business Models and Commercial Viability of Open Hardware Companies

Research literature documents several viable business models for open-source hardware firms. These include: (1) kit and component sales, (2) specialty component manufacturing, (3) consulting and integration services, (4) trademark licensing, (5) subscription services, (6) education and training, (7) secondary supplier/complementary market strategies, and (8) validation and certification services (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000045). Li and Seering (2019) studied 31 open-source hardware firms over an average of 2.3 years and identified a four-phase growth pattern: starting the firm, identifying core competencies, business model improvement, and business maturation (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033).

The following table summarizes financial and strategic data for prominent open hardware companies:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

**Arduino** is the archetypal open hardware success. Founded in 2005 with an initial investment of €3,000, it grew from 200 boards to over 150,000 by Q1 2010 (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000039). Arduino's designs are released under Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike licensing, while the Arduino trademark is protected to maintain brand quality and generate licensing revenue. By 2013, trademark fees constituted approximately 10% of total revenue (pqac-00000033). The founders' primary income derived from consulting for clients developing Arduino-based products, while the growing community contributed free improvements and technical support (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000042).

**SparkFun Electronics** grew from $846,881 in revenue in 2005 to $4 million in 2007 and nearly $7 million in 2008 (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000043). SparkFun's CEO argued that companies relying too heavily on intellectual property become "intellectually unfit" and that continuous innovation outpaces cloners—by the time competitors clone a board and list it on eBay, SparkFun already has the next version in the pipeline (pqac-00000045).

**MakerBot vs. Aleph Objects/LulzBot** provides a natural experiment in open vs. closed strategies. MakerBot was acquired by Stratasys in 2013 for **$403 million** but subsequently abandoned its open-source model, provoking community backlash, boycotts, and reverse-engineering efforts (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000050). Its proprietary "Smart Extruder" led to a class-action lawsuit, and the company experienced sharply declining sales, layoffs, outsourced manufacturing, and retail closures, selling only 1,421 printers during the cited period (pqac-00000049). By contrast, **Aleph Objects** (LulzBot), which maintained its open-source model, reported **$5.8 million in Q2 2016 revenue**, four consecutive profitable quarters, 83% year-over-year revenue growth, **2,782% three-year revenue growth**, and ranked **#122 on the 2016 Inc. 500** with 146 employees (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000049).

**Prusa Research**, founded in Prague in 2012 from the RepRap movement, grew into a substantial enterprise. By 2024, five operating companies reported combined revenue of approximately **CZK 6.6 billion** (roughly USD $280 million) before intra-group eliminations, the group processed about 300,000 orders per year, and employed more than 1,000 people (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000053). Prusa Manufacturing's revenue rose from CZK 1.687 billion to CZK 2.116 billion in 2024, with operating profit increasing from CZK 9.5 million to CZK 66.3 million (pqac-00000051). However, Prusa's openness has become increasingly layered: while software, firmware, and printed-part files are published, some manufacturing data and bills of materials are withheld, and its newer Open Community License restricts commercial resale (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000052).

**Opentrons** is identified in the literature as a commercial vendor of open-source liquid-handling robots serving laboratory automation, representing the science-specific segment of the market (pqac-00000035), though detailed financial data were not available in the reviewed academic sources.

### 4. Open Hardware Licensing: The CERN OHL

The **CERN Open Hardware Licence (CERN OHL)** was published in 2011 and was drafted collaboratively by CERN engineer Javier Serrano and legal expert Myriam Ayass. It was built upon the earlier Tucson Amateur Packet Radio (TAPR) Open Hardware License, which was designed primarily for digital telecommunication devices (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000020). As the concept of "open hardware" expanded beyond electronics to include mechanics, textiles, and other technologies, broader licenses including the CERN OHL and SolderPad License emerged (pqac-00000020).

The CERN OHL was designed to give licensees rights to study, extend, and commercially use digital designs while imposing conditions on derivative works (pqac-00000016). The license now provides **three sharing variants**: strongly reciprocal (CERN-OHL-S, requiring derivative works to be shared under the same terms), weakly reciprocal (CERN-OHL-W), and permissive (CERN-OHL-P) (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000019). Many prominent open hardware projects, including Arduino, have continued using Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike licenses that predate the establishment of dedicated open-hardware licenses (pqac-00000017).

### 5. OSHWA Certification Trends

The **Open Source Hardware Association (OSHWA)** provides a certification program and maintains a registry of certified open hardware projects, assigning unique identifiers to certified designs. OSHWA certification experienced rapid growth: **977 certified projects** were registered as of August 24, 2020, increasing to **1,601 by July 19, 2021**—a **64% increase** in approximately one year (pqac-00000018). Certification requires separate licenses for a project's design, software, and documentation (pqac-00000017). The OSHWA certification has become an important tool for combating misuse of the "open source" label by companies that do not genuinely release open designs (pqac-00000045).

### 6. Comparison with Open-Source Software Commercialization

Open-source hardware and software commercialization share fundamental principles—community-driven development, collaborative innovation, and service-based revenue models—but differ materially due to the physicality of hardware (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000025). The parallels are most apparent in service models: just as Red Hat grew to a **$1.79 billion/year** company by providing services on top of free and open-source software (pqac-00000045), open hardware firms can sell consulting, training, subscriptions, and support (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000024).

Key differences include:

- **Manufacturing costs**: Software has near-zero marginal cost of distribution, while hardware requires physical production, inventory, storage, and distribution (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000027).
- **Licensing limitations**: Copyright provides strong enforcement for software, while many hardware elements are not copyrightable, leaving open-hardware licenses closer to permissive academic licenses. Patent-based reciprocity is possible but costly (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000047).
- **Regulatory compliance**: Commercial hardware must meet EMC, RoHS, CE, and FCC regulations, imposing compliance costs absent from most software (pqac-00000025).
- **Tool heterogeneity**: Hardware development requires expensive, specialized CAD tools, making collaboration harder than with text-based software source code (pqac-00000025).
- **Interdependence**: 86% of open-source hardware market offers were enabled by projects that depended on open-source software, and 96% of surveyed OSH companies had at least one offer enabled by projects using highly restrictive licenses (pqac-00000021).

A survey of open hardware market offers found that hardware-specific revenue categories—finished products, tools, parts, and kits—have no direct open-source software equivalents, while both sectors share revenue from documentation, support, training, and licensing (pqac-00000021). The principal OSH-specific advantage is that intellectual-property cost constitutes a lower proportion of total product cost compared to software, since manufacturing contributes substantially to expenses, reducing the relative impact of open-sourcing the design (pqac-00000021).

### 7. Broader Market Context and Future Directions

The open-source hardware market collectively reached tens of millions of dollars in revenue by 2010, when roughly a dozen startups together made approximately $50 million (pqac-00000031). Li and Seering (2019) found through interviews with 37 open-source hardware company leaders and 12 community members that community building is a key element of firm success—it increases customer-perceived value, decreases product development and sales costs, shortens go-to-market time, and incubates startups with knowledge and resources (pqac-00000032). These advantages can compensate for the risks associated with open-source strategies, making open design a viable product development approach for hardware startups.

However, significant challenges remain. The lack of strong IP protection means cloning is a persistent threat, as demonstrated by MakerBot's experience and the broader pattern of Chinese manufacturers replicating open designs at lower cost (pqac-00000050). Some firms, including Prusa Research, have responded by adopting layered openness—publishing some elements while withholding manufacturing data and imposing restrictions on commercial use (pqac-00000038). Open hardware funding also remains challenging; most scientific hardware development funding follows proprietary models, creating a gap between scientists' ability to purchase expensive proprietary equipment and their inability to finance lower-cost open alternatives (pqac-00000035).

In summary, the research literature demonstrates that open-source scientific hardware can deliver cost savings of 87–94% on average, generate ROI of hundreds to thousands of percent for public funders, and support profitable commercial enterprises ranging from small component sellers to companies with over 1,000 employees and hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue. The field continues to mature through evolving licensing frameworks (CERN OHL), growing certification programs (OSHWA), and business models that adapt open-source software commercialization strategies to the unique challenges of physical products."}

{"answer": "## Economics and Commercialization of Open-Source Hardware: A Literature Review

### 1. Cost Savings of Open-Source Scientific Hardware

A substantial body of work, led primarily by Joshua Pearce, has quantified the economic advantages of free and open-source hardware (FOSH) for scientific and laboratory applications. A comprehensive review of 119 open-source hardware articles from the HardwareX and PLOS Open Source Toolkit repositories found that FOSH provides **average savings of 87%** compared with functionally equivalent proprietary equipment (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003). Savings varied by enabling technology: devices built with Arduino-based electronics averaged **89% savings**, those using RepRap-class 3-D printing averaged **92%**, and devices combining both technologies averaged **94%** (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003). These figures compare direct material costs against commercial purchase prices and may understate total value because proprietary cost equivalents were available for only 37.8% of the reviewed devices—some open-source tools had no commercial counterpart (pqac-00000002).

Individual case studies show even more dramatic savings. An open-source spectrophotometer alternative costing $6 replaced a $1,113 commercial system (~99.5% savings), a multi-fluorescence imaging system costing $250 replaced $10,000 equipment (97.5%), and an open-source selective laser sintering system at $10,000 replaced a $400,000 proprietary system (97.5%) (pqac-00000004). An educational optics setup costing approximately $500 replaced $15,000 of commercial equipment, a 96.7% reduction that, if scaled nationally, could save more than $66 million across U.S. physics laboratories, more than $500 million across U.S. secondary schools, and over $1 billion globally (pqac-00000001).

The following table summarizes documented cost comparisons:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

### 2. Return on Investment for Open-Source Scientific Hardware Development

Pearce (2016) demonstrated that publicly funded open-source hardware development can yield extraordinary returns on investment. Using an open-source syringe pump library as a case study, the development cost was estimated at approximately $30,000. Based on download statistics and estimated savings of $153–$1,402 for a single pump and $1,636–$2,442 for a double pump, the total value of the design library exceeded $168,000 within one month and reached more than $2.5 million within one year. This corresponded to calculated ROI values of **460% to more than 8,300%**. When the 52% national-average overhead typically charged to conventional equipment was included, the ROI increased to **750% to more than 12,000%** (pqac-00000000). The study characterized these as conservative estimates because they excluded benefits from improved equipment, education, and scientific productivity.

Pearce (2026) further analyzed four financial models for open hardware development: (1) a philanthropy model where funders bear all design risks; (2) a standard investor model; (3) a crowd-sourced model; and (4) a novel "decoupled risk investor model" that separates design risk from ROI risk by introducing a guarantor. In a hypothetical case study, 100 proprietary bottle rollers costing $2,439 each ($243,925 total) could be replaced with open-source units at approximately $150 each after a $100,000 development investment, saving over $100,000 (pqac-00000035). The article argues that FOSH reduces costs generally by **more than 90%** for equivalent or lesser proprietary hardware while accelerating development through collaborative design (pqac-00000035).

### 3. Business Models and Commercial Viability of Open Hardware Companies

Research literature documents several viable business models for open-source hardware firms. These include: (1) kit and component sales, (2) specialty component manufacturing, (3) consulting and integration services, (4) trademark licensing, (5) subscription services, (6) education and training, (7) secondary supplier/complementary market strategies, and (8) validation and certification services (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000045). Li and Seering (2019) studied 31 open-source hardware firms over an average of 2.3 years and identified a four-phase growth pattern: starting the firm, identifying core competencies, business model improvement, and business maturation (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033).

The following table summarizes financial and strategic data for prominent open hardware companies:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

**Arduino** is the archetypal open hardware success. Founded in 2005 with an initial investment of €3,000, it grew from 200 boards to over 150,000 by Q1 2010 (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000039). Arduino's designs are released under Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike licensing, while the Arduino trademark is protected to maintain brand quality and generate licensing revenue. By 2013, trademark fees constituted approximately 10% of total revenue (pqac-00000033). The founders' primary income derived from consulting for clients developing Arduino-based products, while the growing community contributed free improvements and technical support (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000042).

**SparkFun Electronics** grew from $846,881 in revenue in 2005 to $4 million in 2007 and nearly $7 million in 2008 (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000043). SparkFun's CEO argued that companies relying too heavily on intellectual property become "intellectually unfit" and that continuous innovation outpaces cloners—by the time competitors clone a board and list it on eBay, SparkFun already has the next version in the pipeline (pqac-00000045).

**MakerBot vs. Aleph Objects/LulzBot** provides a natural experiment in open vs. closed strategies. MakerBot was acquired by Stratasys in 2013 for **$403 million** but subsequently abandoned its open-source model, provoking community backlash, boycotts, and reverse-engineering efforts (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000050). Its proprietary "Smart Extruder" led to a class-action lawsuit, and the company experienced sharply declining sales, layoffs, outsourced manufacturing, and retail closures, selling only 1,421 printers during the cited period (pqac-00000049). By contrast, **Aleph Objects** (LulzBot), which maintained its open-source model, reported **$5.8 million in Q2 2016 revenue**, four consecutive profitable quarters, 83% year-over-year revenue growth, **2,782% three-year revenue growth**, and ranked **#122 on the 2016 Inc. 500** with 146 employees (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000049).

**Prusa Research**, founded in Prague in 2012 from the RepRap movement, grew into a substantial enterprise. By 2024, five operating companies reported combined revenue of approximately **CZK 6.6 billion** (roughly USD $280 million) before intra-group eliminations, the group processed about 300,000 orders per year, and employed more than 1,000 people (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000053). Prusa Manufacturing's revenue rose from CZK 1.687 billion to CZK 2.116 billion in 2024, with operating profit increasing from CZK 9.5 million to CZK 66.3 million (pqac-00000051). However, Prusa's openness has become increasingly layered: while software, firmware, and printed-part files are published, some manufacturing data and bills of materials are withheld, and its newer Open Community License restricts commercial resale (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000052).

**Opentrons** is identified in the literature as a commercial vendor of open-source liquid-handling robots serving laboratory automation, representing the science-specific segment of the market (pqac-00000035), though detailed financial data were not available in the reviewed academic sources.

### 4. Open Hardware Licensing: The CERN OHL

The **CERN Open Hardware Licence (CERN OHL)** was published in 2011 and was drafted collaboratively by CERN engineer Javier Serrano and legal expert Myriam Ayass. It was built upon the earlier Tucson Amateur Packet Radio (TAPR) Open Hardware License, which was designed primarily for digital telecommunication devices (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000020). As the concept of "open hardware" expanded beyond electronics to include mechanics, textiles, and other technologies, broader licenses including the CERN OHL and SolderPad License emerged (pqac-00000020).

The CERN OHL was designed to give licensees rights to study, extend, and commercially use digital designs while imposing conditions on derivative works (pqac-00000016). The license now provides **three sharing variants**: strongly reciprocal (CERN-OHL-S, requiring derivative works to be shared under the same terms), weakly reciprocal (CERN-OHL-W), and permissive (CERN-OHL-P) (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000019). Many prominent open hardware projects, including Arduino, have continued using Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike licenses that predate the establishment of dedicated open-hardware licenses (pqac-00000017).

### 5. OSHWA Certification Trends

The **Open Source Hardware Association (OSHWA)** provides a certification program and maintains a registry of certified open hardware projects, assigning unique identifiers to certified designs. OSHWA certification experienced rapid growth: **977 certified projects** were registered as of August 24, 2020, increasing to **1,601 by July 19, 2021**—a **64% increase** in approximately one year (pqac-00000018). Certification requires separate licenses for a project's design, software, and documentation (pqac-00000017). The OSHWA certification has become an important tool for combating misuse of the "open source" label by companies that do not genuinely release open designs (pqac-00000045).

### 6. Comparison with Open-Source Software Commercialization

Open-source hardware and software commercialization share fundamental principles—community-driven development, collaborative innovation, and service-based revenue models—but differ materially due to the physicality of hardware (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000025). The parallels are most apparent in service models: just as Red Hat grew to a **$1.79 billion/year** company by providing services on top of free and open-source software (pqac-00000045), open hardware firms can sell consulting, training, subscriptions, and support (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000024).

Key differences include:

- **Manufacturing costs**: Software has near-zero marginal cost of distribution, while hardware requires physical production, inventory, storage, and distribution (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000027).
- **Licensing limitations**: Copyright provides strong enforcement for software, while many hardware elements are not copyrightable, leaving open-hardware licenses closer to permissive academic licenses. Patent-based reciprocity is possible but costly (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000047).
- **Regulatory compliance**: Commercial hardware must meet EMC, RoHS, CE, and FCC regulations, imposing compliance costs absent from most software (pqac-00000025).
- **Tool heterogeneity**: Hardware development requires expensive, specialized CAD tools, making collaboration harder than with text-based software source code (pqac-00000025).
- **Interdependence**: 86% of open-source hardware market offers were enabled by projects that depended on open-source software, and 96% of surveyed OSH companies had at least one offer enabled by projects using highly restrictive licenses (pqac-00000021).

A survey of open hardware market offers found that hardware-specific revenue categories—finished products, tools, parts, and kits—have no direct open-source software equivalents, while both sectors share revenue from documentation, support, training, and licensing (pqac-00000021). The principal OSH-specific advantage is that intellectual-property cost constitutes a lower proportion of total product cost compared to software, since manufacturing contributes substantially to expenses, reducing the relative impact of open-sourcing the design (pqac-00000021).

### 7. Broader Market Context and Future Directions

The open-source hardware market collectively reached tens of millions of dollars in revenue by 2010, when roughly a dozen startups together made approximately $50 million (pqac-00000031). Li and Seering (2019) found through interviews with 37 open-source hardware company leaders and 12 community members that community building is a key element of firm success—it increases customer-perceived value, decreases product development and sales costs, shortens go-to-market time, and incubates startups with knowledge and resources (pqac-00000032). These advantages can compensate for the risks associated with open-source strategies, making open design a viable product development approach for hardware startups.

However, significant challenges remain. The lack of strong IP protection means cloning is a persistent threat, as demonstrated by MakerBot's experience and the broader pattern of Chinese manufacturers replicating open designs at lower cost (pqac-00000050). Some firms, including Prusa Research, have responded by adopting layered openness—publishing some elements while withholding manufacturing data and imposing restrictions on commercial use (pqac-00000038). Open hardware funding also remains challenging; most scientific hardware development funding follows proprietary models, creating a gap between scientists' ability to purchase expensive proprietary equipment and their inability to finance lower-cost open alternatives (pqac-00000035).

In summary, the research literature demonstrates that open-source scientific hardware can deliver cost savings of 87–94% on average, generate ROI of hundreds to thousands of percent for public funders, and support profitable commercial enterprises ranging from small component sellers to companies with over 1,000 employees and hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue. The field continues to mature through evolving licensing frameworks (CERN OHL), growing certification programs (OSHWA), and business models that adapt open-source software commercialization strategies to the unique challenges of physical products."}

The founders' primary income derived from consulting for clients developing Arduino-based products, while the growing community contributed free improvements and technical support (thompson2011buildit.share pages 1-4, thompson2011buildit.share pages 4-6).

**SparkFun Electronics** grew from $846,881 in revenue in 2005 to $4 million in 2007 and nearly $7 million in 2008 (cruz2017exploringtheopen pages 159-162, cruz2017exploringtheopena pages 159-162). SparkFun's CEO argued that companies relying too heavily on intellectual property become "intellectually unfit" and that continuous innovation outpaces cloners—by the time competitors clone a board and list it on eBay, SparkFun already has the next version in the pipeline (pearce2017emergingbusinessmodels pages 6-7).

**MakerBot vs. Aleph Objects/LulzBot** provides a natural experiment in open vs. closed strategies. MakerBot was acquired by Stratasys in 2013 for **$403 million** but subsequently abandoned its open-source model, provoking community backlash, boycotts, and reverse-engineering efforts (pearce2017emergingbusinessmodels pages 8-9, viseur20223dprinterbuilders’ pages 3-4). Its proprietary "Smart Extruder" led to a class-action lawsuit, and the company experienced sharply declining sales, layoffs, outsourced manufacturing, and retail closures, selling only 1,421 printers during the cited period (pearce2017emergingbusinessmodels pages 8-9). By contrast, **Aleph Objects** (LulzBot), which maintained its open-source model, reported **$5.8 million in Q2 2016 revenue**, four consecutive profitable quarters, 83% year-over-year revenue growth, **2,782% three-year revenue growth**, and ranked **#122 on the 2016 Inc. 500** with 146 employees (pearce2017emergingbusinessmodels pages 8-9).

**Prusa Research**, founded in Prague in 2012 from the RepRap movement, grew into a substantial enterprise. By 2024, five operating companies reported combined revenue of approximately **CZK 6.6 billion** (roughly USD $280 million) before intra-group eliminations, the group processed about 300,000 orders per year, and employed more than 1,000 people (guhathakurta2026prusa3dsopensourcemanufacturing pages 1-4). Prusa Manufacturing's revenue rose from CZK 1.687 billion to CZK 2.116 billion in 2024, with operating profit increasing from CZK 9.5 million to CZK 66.3 million (guhathakurta2026prusa3dsopensourcemanufacturing pages 9-12). However, Prusa's openness has become increasingly layered: while software, firmware, and printed-part files are published, some manufacturing data and bills of materials are withheld, and its newer Open Community License restricts commercial resale (guhathakurta2026prusa3dsopensourcemanufacturing pages 4-7, viseur20223dprinterbuilders’ pages 4-5).

**Opentrons** is identified in the literature as a commercial vendor of open-source liquid-handling robots serving laboratory automation, representing the science-specific segment of the market (pearce2026deriskingthefinance pages 3-7), though detailed financial data were not available in the reviewed academic sources.

### 4. Open Hardware Licensing: The CERN OHL

The **CERN Open Hardware Licence (CERN OHL)** was published in 2011 and was drafted collaboratively by CERN engineer Javier Serrano and legal expert Myriam Ayass. It was built upon the earlier Tucson Amateur Packet Radio (TAPR) Open Hardware License, which was designed primarily for digital telecommunication devices (murillo2018assemblingopenhardware pages 4-8, bonvoisin2020standardisationofpractices pages 1-3). As the concept of "open hardware" expanded beyond electronics to include mechanics, textiles, and other technologies, broader licenses including the CERN OHL and SolderPad License emerged (bonvoisin2020standardisationofpractices pages 1-3).

The CERN OHL was designed to give licensees rights to study, extend, and commercially use digital designs while imposing conditions on derivative works (murillo2018assemblingopenhardware pages 4-8). The **Open Source Hardware Association (OSHWA)** provides a certification program and maintains a registry of certified open hardware projects, assigning unique identifiers to certified designs. OSHWA certification experienced rapid growth: **977 certified projects** were registered as of August 24, 2020, increasing to **1,601 by July 19, 2021**—a **64% increase** in approximately one year (miljkovic2109towardsfairprinciples pages 1-3). Certification requires separate licenses for a project's design, software, and documentation (miljkovic2109towardsfairprinciples pages 3-6). The OSHWA certification has become an important tool for combating misuse of the "open source" label by companies that do not genuinely release open designs (pearce2017emergingbusinessmodels pages 6-7).

The parallels are most apparent in service models: just as Red Hat grew to a **$1.79 billion/year** company by providing services on top of free and open-source software (pearce2017emergingbusinessmodels pages 6-7), open hardware firms can sell consulting, training, subscriptions, and support (parker2021thepotentialfor pages 13-16, mies2024potentialandchallenges pages 88-90).

- **Manufacturing costs**: Software has near-zero marginal cost of distribution, while hardware requires physical production, inventory, storage, and distribution (lock2013opensourcehardwarecan pages 25-28, lock2013opensourcehardwarecan pages 13-19).
- **Licensing limitations**: Copyright provides strong enforcement for software, while many hardware elements are not copyrightable, leaving open-hardware licenses closer to permissive academic licenses. - **Regulatory compliance**: Commercial hardware must meet EMC, RoHS, CE, and FCC regulations, imposing compliance costs absent from most software (lock2013opensourcehardwarecan pages 25-28).
- **Tool heterogeneity**: Hardware development requires expensive, specialized CAD tools, making collaboration harder than with text-based software source code (lock2013opensourcehardwarecan pages 25-28).
- **Interdependence**: 86% of open-source hardware market offers were enabled by projects that depended on open-source software, and 96% of surveyed OSH companies had at least one offer enabled by projects using highly restrictive licenses (ferreira2010typesofmarket pages 69-76).

### 7. Broader Market Context and Future Directions

The open-source hardware market collectively reached tens of millions of dollars in revenue by 2010, when roughly a dozen startups together made approximately $50 million (cruz2017exploringtheopen pages 27-30). Li and Seering (2019) found through interviews with 37 open-source hardware company leaders and 12 community members that community building is a key element of firm success—it increases customer-perceived value, decreases product development and sales costs, shortens go-to-market time, and incubates startups with knowledge and resources (li2019buildyourfirm pages 7-8). These advantages can compensate for the risks associated with open-source strategies, making open design a viable product development approach for hardware startups.

However, significant challenges remain. The lack of strong IP protection means cloning is a persistent threat, as demonstrated by MakerBot's experience and the broader pattern of Chinese manufacturers replicating open designs at lower cost (viseur20223dprinterbuilders’ pages 3-4). ## Economics and Commercialization of Open-Source Hardware: A Literature Review

### 1. Cost Savings of Open-Source Scientific Hardware

A substantial body of work, led primarily by Joshua Pearce, has quantified the economic advantages of free and open-source hardware (FOSH) for scientific and laboratory applications. A comprehensive review of 119 open-source hardware articles from the HardwareX and PLOS Open Source Toolkit repositories found that FOSH provides **average savings of 87%** compared with functionally equivalent proprietary equipment (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003). Savings varied by enabling technology: devices built with Arduino-based electronics averaged **89% savings**, those using RepRap-class 3-D printing averaged **92%**, and devices combining both technologies averaged **94%** (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003). These figures compare direct material costs against commercial purchase prices and may understate total value because proprietary cost equivalents were available for only 37.8% of the reviewed devices—some open-source tools had no commercial counterpart (pqac-00000002).

Individual case studies show even more dramatic savings. An open-source spectrophotometer alternative costing $6 replaced a $1,113 commercial system (~99.5% savings), a multi-fluorescence imaging system costing $250 replaced $10,000 equipment (97.5%), and an open-source selective laser sintering system at $10,000 replaced a $400,000 proprietary system (97.5%) (pqac-00000004). An educational optics setup costing approximately $500 replaced $15,000 of commercial equipment, a 96.7% reduction that, if scaled nationally, could save more than $66 million across U.S. physics laboratories, more than $500 million across U.S. secondary schools, and over $1 billion globally (pqac-00000001).

Pearce (2016) demonstrated that publicly funded open-source hardware development can yield extraordinary returns on investment. The documented percentage figures are therefore ROI measures, indicating that returns were several times the original development investment. The article also characterizes these estimates as conservative because they count primarily direct replacement savings and exclude additional benefits such as improved equipment, education, and scientific productivity.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides commercial evidence primarily for MakerBot and LulzBot’s parent company, Aleph Objects, rather than for Arduino, Adafruit, SparkFun, Prusa Research, or Opentrons. MakerBot was acquired by Stratasys in 2013 for $403 million, but its subsequent shift away from open-hardware practices damaged community support. The passage associates this proprietary pivot with poor product performance, a class-action lawsuit concerning the Smart Extruder, sharply declining sales, layoffs, outsourcing manufacturing to China, and closure of retail locations. In the comparison presented, Aleph Objects—manufacturer of LulzBot products and continuing with an open-source model—reported US$5.8 million in revenue in the second quarter of 2016, four consecutive profitable quarters, and 83% year-over-year revenue growth. It achieved 2,782% three-year revenue growth and ranked #122 in the 2016 Inc. 500. Aleph Objects had 146 employees and operated 155 self-replicating manufacturing machines in the United States, while expanding distribution through warehouses in the UK, Canada, and Australia to serve customers in more than 85 countries. By contrast, MakerBot sold only 1,421 printers during the cited period and undertook substantial staff reductions. The excerpt therefore suggests that open-source hardware can support profitable commercial operations, but it does not provide business models or revenue figures for the other named companies.

SparkFun presents open source as both an ethical and practical strategy: releasing materials openly reduces concern about patents and lawyers, supports collaboration, and can still make strong business sense. The text identifies a principal OSHW model as selling hardware while generating income through support, service, or customization. Arduino and SparkFun are cited as contrasting successful examples: SparkFun primarily sells individual devices, whereas Arduino’s founders primarily earned income from client integration work and consulting. The excerpt emphasizes commercial risks, especially weak licensing protection, low-cost clones, and the need to recover development costs. Companies can defend sales through branding, trademarks, manufacturing quality, continuous product updates, and new product development. It also notes that community integration may create compliance-testing costs, although modular add-on boards can limit the need to recertify a main product. contexts.context: The excerpt primarily describes commercialization for open source hardware and offers only a limited comparison with open source software. A key similarity is that both can generate value without relying exclusively on conventional intellectual-property protection: open source companies may monetize products, services, brands, customization, support, or complementary markets. The text specifically notes that hardware business models resemble those of open source software companies such as Red Hat, especially through service-based revenue. Hardware commercialization, however, faces distinctive physical-production and distribution challenges. Designers may differ from manufacturers and distributors, requiring business models that capture value across multiple actors. Hardware firms may sell finished devices, kits, parts, customized products, or hardware-as-a-service, while also earning revenue from support, education, and training. Open hardware can additionally stimulate complementary demand, as with an open photometer that increased demand for related enzymes. Funding and manufacturing costs are also central: hardware projects may use crowdfunding, grants, group purchasing, small-batch production, or self-funding. By contrast, the excerpt does not provide detailed software-specific commercialization mechanisms, but implies that software has more established service-oriented analogues. Thus, the strongest evidence supports shared openness and service/complementary-market strategies, alongside hardware-specific costs, logistics, physical products, and educational services.
contexts.question: How do open source hardware and open source software commercialization models compare? What are the key differences and similarities?

contexts.context:
The excerpt presents open source hardware (OSH) and open source software (OSS) commercialization as similar in their reliance on open projects, licensing, and complementary commercial offers. Both can generate revenue through products, tools, documentation, support, training, commercial licensing, and brand-based offerings. Highly restrictive licensing is especially important: 96% of the surveyed OSH companies had at least one offer enabled by an OSH project using such a license, paralleling the licensing practices observed in OSS. OSH also frequently depends on OSS: 86% of OSH market offers were enabled by OSH projects that depended on OSS, and some OSH projects were based on external OSH projects.

The key difference is physicality. OSS is intangible, while OSH produces tangible artifacts requiring manufacturing. This enables OSH-specific market categories—hardware based on OSH designs, hardware tools, and parts or kits—that have no direct OSS equivalents. OSH development tools tend to be more expensive and specialized, whereas software tools tend to be cheaper and more generic. OSH also has a lower proportion of intellectual-property cost relative to product cost because manufacturing contributes substantially to expenses. Finally, OSH products generally require distribution channels different from those used to distribute source code, while OSS products use the same channels as source-code distribution.

contexts.context: The excerpt presents open source hardware (OSHW) as modeled on open source software (OSS), with both based on publicly available source material and user freedoms to study, modify, improve, distribute, and commercially use derivative works. In both domains, openness prioritizes the right to distribute and share knowledge rather than the right to exclude others, and both can support commerce through open exchange. The central commercialization difference is that OSS primarily distributes intangible code, whereas OSHW involves physical products. Software modification generally requires only an ordinary computer and has virtually no distribution cost, allowing copying and redistribution at very low marginal cost. Hardware commercialization must account for manufacturing, components, materials, assembly, testing, logistics, and potentially regulatory requirements. The excerpt also indicates that OSS licenses are grounded largely in copyright law and can directly regulate how code is used, while hardware-related legal and practical controls do not always map neatly onto copyright. OSHW therefore makes the design files open, but producing and selling the resulting device still requires physical resources. The report focuses on identifying feasible business models, limitations, and potential gains for embedded-electronics companies using or developing OSHW, while noting that its proposed business models were not tested in the study.

contexts.context: The excerpt presents open source hardware (OSHW) and open source software (OSS) as sharing a commercialization philosophy based on publicly available source materials, freedom to study and modify designs, redistribution, derivative works, and community collaboration. This openness can support broad adoption, improvements, and commerce; OSHW is explicitly defined as allowing people to “make, and sell” designs or hardware based on them. Commercialization nevertheless differs substantially because OSHW concerns physical products. Hardware has unavoidable manufacturing, inventory, storage, and distribution costs, whereas software can be distributed online at nearly no marginal cost. Software can also be updated automatically, while hardware changes require physical replacement. OSHW development may require expensive specialized equipment and depends on heterogeneous, often proprietary CAD tools, making collaboration and modification harder than working with text-based software source code. Software versions can commonly be compared and merged automatically; PCB and other hardware designs generally cannot. Licensing is another difference: copyright provides stronger and more established enforcement for OSS, while many hardware elements are not copyrightable, so OSHW licenses often resemble permissive academic licenses; patent-based reciprocity is possible but costly and limited. Estimates depend heavily on downloaders actually fabricating devices and extrapolations; 5-year market capture was projected at $767 million annual savings.

contexts.context: The excerpt states that MakerBot was purchased by Stratasys in 2013 for $403 million. After MakerBot moved away from the Open Hardware ethos, it reportedly lost community support and faced customer outrage over licensing changes on Thingiverse, attempts to patent freely uploaded designs, deletion of documentation, and the release of proprietary printers and software. Its proprietary “Smart Extruder” was described as a major engineering failure that led to a class-action lawsuit, while subsequent operational failures contributed to sharply declining sales, layoffs, outsourcing of U.S. manufacturing, and closure of retail locations. contexts.context: The excerpt describes MakerBot’s transition from RepRap-derived open hardware to a proprietary strategy. MakerBot was incorporated in 2009 to commercialize open designs, but by September 2012 its Replicator 2 was released under a proprietary license. The company also pursued patents beginning in 2010, changed its model-sharing platform’s terms to transfer ownership of creators’ designs to MakerBot, and increasingly relied on proprietary technological assets and a professional-market strategy. The shift provoked opposition from the RepRap community, including calls for a boycott, a halt to contributions, and reverse engineering of proprietary machines. The text attributes the strategic reversal mainly to value-capture difficulties, including losses of low-cost desktop-printer market share to Chinese manufacturers and slower-than-expected market growth. It characterizes MakerBot’s later approach as essentially proprietary, aside from older open-source software and firmware, and compares it with a razor-and-blade model centered on patented modular extruders and associated materials. The excerpt also states that Ultimaker scaled successfully while progressively closing its hardware development process.
